newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open higher before June CPI report.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open higher before June CPI report.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened higher on Wednesday ahead of what is expected to be a market-friendly June Consumer Price Index (CPI) report.
Economists polled by Reuters forecast that the CPI, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, rose 0.2 percent in June after rising 0.1 percent in May.
Without its food and energy components, the core CPI is believed to have also risen 0.2 percent in June after rising 0.2 percent in May.
Those readings would keep the trailing 12 months CPI near 2.2 percent, below the 2.4 percent CPI growth in 1996, and would have a benign affect on the market, analysts said.
A smaller than expected CPI increase could boost prices. A surprising increase of 0.3 percent or more would set the market back from current levels, analysts said.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond opened at 101-5/32, up 4/32 to yield 6.54 percent on Wednesday.
Three- and six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.06 percent and 5.11 percent, respectively. Year bill rates were up one basis point to 5.23 percent.
Two-year notes were unchanged at 100-5/32, yielding 5.91 percent. Five-year notes were up 2/32 to 100-14/32, yielding 6.15 percent and ten-year notes were up 2/32 to 102-24/32, yielding 6.25 percent.

Analysts said lower energy and gold prices, productivity gains, a weak global economy and a strong dollar have restrained the price increases recorded by the CPI, offsetting factors like strong U.S. economic growth and low unemployment that could foster wage and price spirals.
Other economic data is also on tap for the market on Wednesday.
At 0915 EDT/1315 GMT, the Federal Reserve will release is industrial production and capacity utilization data for June.

Those data are expected to show that output edged up 0.2 percent in June after rising 0.4 percent in May and that capacity use -- the portion of the nation's factories, mines and utilities employed in that production -- eased to 83.6 percent from 83.7 percent.

Analysts said a drop in the length of the average workweek recorded in the Labor Department's June employment report pointed to lower production but that the "unwinding" of the effects of spring auto strikes would tend to boost it.
At the same time that the CPI comes out, the government will also release May business inventories data.
Business inventories are calculated to have risen 0.3 percent in May after increasing 0.3 percent in April, according to economists polled by Reuters.

U.S. real earnings for June are due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. No forecast was available for that report. Real earnings rose 0.3 percent in May. The data are unlikely to have a market impact, analysts said.
Matthew Alexy, chief markets strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston, said the market could grind higher today and for the rest of the week.
If the CPI comes in as expected, up 0.2 percent, "there will be a little bit of relief," said Alexy.
Another positive is that the market "did pretty well overnight," he said.

"If you get past CPI, there's nothing important standing in the way of the market for the rest of the week," Alexy said. "We'll go up and test 114-15 (on the September T-bond futures contract) and 6.51 percent (on the bond yield.)"
